DUBAI—A projectile launched by Yemen ’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels struck the tallest tower in Saudi Arabia ’s capital Thursday, causing damage across multiple floors of a building home to the kingdom’s sovereign-wealth fund.
The strike on the Public Investment Fund Tower, which stands over Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District, follows a previous Houthi strike on the neighborhood that is home to some of the world’s biggest financial firms.

articles.title_zh: China gives Japan PM frosty welcome at Apec amid fanfare for other leaders
articles.content_orig:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here
The Associated Press is reporting that Donald Trump plans to hold a meeting with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, citing an anonymous US official. The meeting would be in addition to the blockbuster trilateral talks the two will hold with host Xi Jinping on Thursday.
Meanwhile, a meeting between the leaders of China, the United States and Russia planned for Thursday in Shenzhen is set to last less than 60 minutes, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media on Wednesday. “No more than an hour” has been set aside for the historic summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian state news agencies.
Xi Jinping told Donald Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a “constructive, strategic and stable relationship” between China and the US, based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua . Xi also recalled Trump’s personal welcome at the airport during his visit to the US in September, saying China’s own welcome for the US president reflected its tradition of reciprocity.
Xi personally greeted Trump on the airport tarmac in Shenzhen , reciprocating the welcome the US president extended to the Chinese leader during his visit to the US in September.
Before landing in Shenzhen, Donald Trump enjoyed lunch in Manila with Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr at the Malacañang presidential palace. Speaking during a meeting ahead of lunch, Marcos revealed that he had arranged for fried chicken from Filipino fast food chain Jollibee to be delivered to the US delegation as a late-night snack last night, praising Trump for “working very hard”.
Chinese state media have released a readout of Xi Jinping’s earlier meeting with Vladimir Putin . In it, Xi is quoted as saying China-Russia relations are “unshaken by storms and steady as a mountain”, and have set “an example of a new type of major-country relationship characterised by equality, mutual respect, trustworthiness, and win-win co-operation”.
Canada’s Mark Carney has hit back at Vladimir Putin’s earlier assertion that sanctions no longer work in this day and age. “Mr Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he’ll find out that they’re very real, they’re biting,” Carney told reporters.
Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum won praise and went viral on Chinese social media on Wednesday for taking an economy flight to attend a regional summit in Shenzhen. World leaders this week descended on the southern Chinese city to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings – many arriving in specially chartered commercial airliners or dedicated government aircraft like US president Donald Trump’s Air Force One.
It is unclear whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the talks, but Trump has floated the possibility. On Wednesday US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US president was willing to engage, but he did not confirm whether a meeting had been set in Shenzhen.
Trump said on Wednesday that the US has just ⁠concluded a “very big ⁠trade ​deal” with the Philippines, but he did not provide any details, and Manila ⁠did not announce any agreement. “We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the ⁠biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far, and it ​is a fair ‌deal for both countries,” ‌Trump said during a state luncheon at the Philippine ‌presidential palace. Trump is set to arrive in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening.
Trump landed in China on Wednesday seeking to reinforce America’s status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left his administration scrambling to calm the US public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty before the meeting with Xi and Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the US worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
“It’s fine,” Trump said Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is “big and powerful.”
The meeting between the leaders of China , the United States and Russia planned for Thursday in Shenzhen is set to last less than 60 minutes, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media.
“No more than an hour” has been set aside for the historic summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin , Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian state news agencies.
The Associated Press is reporting that Donald Trump plans to hold a separate meeting with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, citing an anonymous US official.
The meeting would be in addition to the blockbuster trilateral talks the two will hold with host Xi Jinping on Thursday.
If confirmed, it would be their first bilateral since they met in Alaska in 2025 for talks that failed to reach a deal on the war in Ukraine.
Trump had already suggested he might meet with Putin, as well as with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, but neither option had been added to his official schedule.
Before landing in Shenzhen, Donald Trump enjoyed lunch in Manila with Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr at the Malacañang presidential palace.
Speaking during a meeting ahead of lunch, Marcos revealed that he had arranged for fried chicken from Filipino fast food chain Jollibee to be delivered to the US delegation as a late-night snack last night, praising Trump for “working very hard”.
The gift may have gone down particularly well with Trump, who has something of a reputation for his love of fast food. The US president has long been associated with McDonald’s and KFC, with his former campaign aides revealing in 2017 that his usual McDonald’s order included two Big Macs, two Filet-O-Fish sandwiches and a chocolate milkshake. The Guardian reported on their revelations at the time in this article:
Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum won praise and went viral on Chinese social media on Wednesday for taking an economy flight to attend a regional summit in Shenzhen.
World leaders this week descended on the southern Chinese city to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings – many arriving in specially chartered commercial airliners or dedicated government aircraft like US president Donald Trump’s Air Force One.
Sheinbaum, however, flew in economy class from Mexico City to Shenzhen on a China Southern Airlines flight, media reports said. She arrived in China on Monday.
Posts on Chinese social media platform Weibo showed the Mexican leader in the plane chatting with passengers, though the photos could not be independently verified by AFP. A hashtag on Weibo about her arrival in China garnered 10.2m views as of Wednesday.
Meanwhile, Sheinbaum said ​on Wednesday she had a “very good ⁠meeting” with her US counterpart Trump ⁠as the two ​countries ‌pursue negotiations aimed ‌at easing trade tensions.
“We ‌continue to make progress on our shared agenda,” Sheinbaum added in a post on ‌X.
The Canadian prime minister’s office has issued a statement following Mark Carney’s meeting with US president Donald Trump on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen.
double quotation mark This evening, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, met with the President of the United States, Donald J. Trump, on the margins of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, in Shenzhen, China.
The leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create good jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty. They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes
Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.
The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.
The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.
Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.
Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel .
In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.
One Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he said. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”
Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention , is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa said during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.
After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, said the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.
The case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.
In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.
Refugees who fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli , where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down , was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.
During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.
The court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.
Myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.
However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
During a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.
The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.
Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel committed acts of genocide in Gaza.
A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay .
Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration . However, the Trump administration has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.
Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkan wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.
Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

articles.title_orig: Stocks making the biggest moves Thursday: Palo Alto Networks, Take-Two Interactive, Everpure, Walmart & more
articles.title_zh: Stocks making the biggest moves Thursday: Palo Alto Networks, Take-Two Interactive, Everpure, Walmart & more
articles.content_orig:
Palo Alto Networks popped in early trading Thursday, boosted by quarterly results that beat analyst expectations. Data storage name Everpure also got a boost after it lifted its fiscal-year outlook.
Follow along as CNBC covers the biggest stock market moves of the day.
Shares of Coherent are up nearly 11%, extending gains after Nvidia 's latest earnings report earlier in the week highlighted continued demand for data-center technology.
Coherent, which supplies optical components used in AI data centers, said its data-center revenue rose 85% year over year in its fiscal first quarter.
On Nov. 18, the company's board authorized a share repurchase program of up to $2 billion . Coherent may buy shares in the open market or through other transactions. The program has no expiration date and does not require the company to repurchase a specific amount.
Shares of the software company making tools for computer chips jumped 3.2% after Barclays initiated coverage with an overweight rating and a $640 price target implying 47% upside from Wednesday's close. Analyst Saket Kalia noted that Synopsys is the leader of a growing Electronic Design Automation (EDA) market, which is driven by rising spend in semiconductor research and development.
MongoDB gained 4% before the bell following an upgrade at UBS to buy from neutral.
The bank's channel checks pointed to steady demand and better-than-expected consumer and partner growth, which should support durable 20%-plus total revenue growth and 25%-plus revenue growth for its cloud database service Atlas over the coming years, analyst Radi Sultan said.
In addition, MongoDB could be utilized in 20% to 40% of incremental AI workloads, which is not fully reflected in the stock's valuation, he said.
Data storage stocks are getting a lift in the premarket Thursday as the Anthropic IPO aims to breathe new life into AI-trade
Shares of Seagate Technology are up more than 6% while Western Digital stock popped 5.8%.
Seagate and Western Digital provide provide mass data storage infrastructure, a crucial role in the AI ecosystem to help AI models run.
The strong momentum around data storage and AI infrastructure demand is already high.
But a large chuck of that demand will come from leading AI lab Anthropic, which is set to go public Thursday.
Chipmakers advanced on Thursday ahead of Anthropic's IPO.
Marvell gained 4.2%, Advanced Micro Devices is up 2.8%, Broadcom advanced 2.5%, Intel moved 4.4% higher and Nvidia is up 1.5%.
These artificial intelligence chips will help Anthropic run Claude models faster.
Leading chipmakers need the IPO to go well, as Anthropic has $900 billion in spending commitments.
Shares of Bloom Energy surged nearly 8% in the premarket Thursday after being upgraded to outperform at BMO Capital Markets.
The analysts cited their endorsement of the company after coming away with positive meetings with management.
The firm however decreased its price target to $230 from $260, which still implies a 35% upside to the stock's Thursday close of $170 per share.
UBS upgraded the intelligent content management provider to buy from neutral, sending shares 3.6% higher in premarket trading.
The firm believes Box 's recent artificial intelligence growth acceleration can support sustained double-digit revenue growth. "Investors have been looking for evidence that AI can drive an inflection in software growth, and Box is increasingly demonstrating exactly that," analyst Taylor McGinnis wrote.
Walmart shares were down more than 1% even after the retail giant reported third-quarter results that beat expectations and raised its full-year guidance.
The company posted adjusted earnings per share of 65 cents on revenue of $188.84 billion. Analysts expected a profit of 64 cents per share on revenue of $187.27 billion.
For the year, Walmart sees net sales rising 4.9% to 5.2%, more than a previous guidance of 4% to 5%.
Shares of Take-Two Interactive slipped 1%, giving back some of their gains from the previous session. The stock popped more than 6% on Wednesday ahead of the release of the much-anticipated "Grand Theft Auto VI" game.
Take-Two is up nearly 14% in November, though the stock has dropped 15% in 2026.
Cybersecurity player Palo Alto Networks advanced 10% after its fiscal first-quarter results came in above the Street's expectations.
The company earned $1.05 per share on an adjusted basis and revenue of $3.44 billion. The LSEG consensus estimate called for 97 cents per share on $3.31 billion of revenue.
Guidance for the fiscal year ending July 2027 calls for adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 per share on revenue of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion. Analysts sought $4.18 per share and $14.16 billion, according to LSEG.
The data management company advanced 5% after raising its guidance for the fiscal-year ending January 2027.
Everpure sees revenue in a range of $5.20 billion to $5.21 billion, up from its earlier call of $5.03 billion to $5.07 billion. Analysts polled by FactSet were looking for $5.06 billion.
Third-quarter results also surpassed estimates on the top and bottom lines.
The manufacturer of power generation equipment pulled back 1%. Woodward expects adjusted earnings for the fiscal year ending September 2027 to range between $10.20 and $10.70 per share, below the FactSet consensus estimate of $10.74 per share.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO Live Updates: AI Firm Set to Begin Trading at $83 a Share Under ANT
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO Live Updates: AI Firm Set to Begin Trading at $83 a Share Under ANT
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Anthropic's debut is the AI payday Wall Street has been waiting for. For the companies that fix broken software, the whole year has been a Y2K -style bonanza.
Anthropic ( ANT ) priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its $70-$78 range. It arrives after weeks of outages at Microsoft ( MSFT ), JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) and Apple ( AAPL ), each blamed on internal problems rather than hackers.
Ben Emons of research firm FedWatch Advisors calls it the "Patchpocalypse." "A flood of AI-found bugs means a flood of patches, and every patch is a chance for something to break," he wrote Wednesday.
Newly reported software security flaws in the federal National Vulnerability Database hit a record high of almost 17,500 in October, about four times the level a year earlier, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. This year's count, more than 100,000, already tops 2024 and 2025 combined.
The surge took off after Anthropic unveiled Claude Mythos Preview on April 7, a bug hunter so strong that Anthropic limited its release to a small group of partners.
Microsoft's models are finding flaws "which humans haven't found for years or even decades," Mustafa Suleyman, who runs Microsoft's AI unit, told Deirdre Bosa on Deirdre Bosa Live.
Fixing them isn't cheap or optional.
Since April 7, CrowdStrike ( CRWD ) and Palo Alto Networks ( PANW ) shares have doubled or better. The First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF ( CIBR ) is up nearly 50%, more than twice tech's gain, and has fallen less since the Oct. 6 tech peak, about 11% vs. nearly 20% for tech ( XLK ).
Palo Alto was surging early Thursday after raising its full-year outlook, lifting other cyber stocks. CEO Nikesh Arora told analysts "unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes" were partly behind the recent outages.
Y2K, short for "year 2000," was the late-1990s fear that computers storing years as two digits would read 2000 as 1900. Fixing it cost US companies and governments more than $100 billion, according to a 1999 Commerce Department estimate. That spending stopped when the clock ran out. This bug hunt has no deadline, since the models keep getting better.
The bug fixers have already been paid. Anthropic's new shareholders are still waiting. Twelve of the 15 larger US IPOs DataTrek Research tracked this year trade below their offer price , and the firm says Anthropic "at least needs a decent first-day gain."
Last year, companies raced to use as much AI as they could, so-called "token maxing." Somesh Dash, a general partner at Anthropic investor IVP, sees this year's race in security operations centers (SOCs), the teams that watch for attacks around the clock.
"If last year was token maxing, this year is going to be SOC maxing," Dash told Deirdre Bosa . He sees the outages as growing pains.
"We're actually doing the really necessary plumbing to be able to prepare for this next generation."

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for a rare 3-way meeting in China, but appear to achieve little
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for a rare 3-way meeting in China, but appear to achieve little
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said the U.S., Russia and China are "uniquely positioned" to reduce the world's nuclear weapons stockpile during his historic trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on Thursday.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on earth and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in opening remarks.
"The power is unbelievable, unthinkable," he said, adding that it's "a very hard thing" for countries to reduce nuclear weapons.
That would include not letting Iran have nuclear weapons, Trump said.
He said the three leaders would also discuss the war between Russia and Ukraine, and criticized "rogue globalist organizations," including the International Criminal Court.
The closely watched meeting ended about an hour and a half after it kicked off late Thursday afternoon, following a working lunch between Trump and Xi that started at least an hour later than originally planned.
Trump told Xi and Putin they were "really making history" with the first-ever trilateral meeting between the the three countries' leaders.
He said it was an "honor" to be at the meeting with Putin and Xi, whom he congratulated on a very successful APEC summit."
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," Trump added. "We feel the opposite."
At the trilateral, Xi said that for large nations, having good interactions is not a choice but a necessity, according to a translation by state media.
In the report, Xi noted China's partnership with Russia, work towards constructive strategic stability in U.S. relations, and called on the three countries to respond to the world's challenges.
Xi laid out four "correct" ways for large countries to interact: mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, and adherence to dialogue, according to state media.
The Chinese president echoed Trump's comments on nuclear weapons, calling for such arms to be comprehensively prohibited and destroyed, adding that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
Putin said Russia, China and the U.S. can strengthen global stability if they cooperate constructively, calling for the three leaders to discuss energy security and global and regional issues — including the war in Ukraine.
Beijing only confirmed the closely watched meeting on Monday. The three leaders had briefly gathered Wednesday evening as part of a welcome banquet for the APEC leaders more broadly.

articles.title_orig: A wave of outages has Americans preparing for doomsday
articles.title_zh: A wave of outages has Americans preparing for doomsday
articles.content_orig:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.
Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies , a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking , this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.
Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.
“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”
So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.
As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”
Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services , for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.
In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.
On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.
It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.
Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS , Google Cloud Platform , and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products , Google Workspace , telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.
When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon —but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net . Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts .
When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.
Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what's actually going on,” she says.
Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.
Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that q

articles.title_orig: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
articles.title_zh: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
articles.content_orig:
Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.
In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.
A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.
But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin said Moscow's response would be even more significant.
Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.
Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles.
From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplied its troops in southern Ukraine.
Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."
The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years.
The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions.
It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea.
Thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.
Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
The seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.
In response to Tuesday's hit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But the operation to repair it could take a long time, and it will likely have to be carried out under frequent Ukrainian fire.
Russia has regularly targeted Ukrainian civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
This week alone, as the Crimean Bridge was being hit, Moscow targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

articles.title_orig: Major KFC franchisee files for bankruptcy, puts 84 restaurants up for sale
articles.title_zh: Major KFC franchisee files for bankruptcy, puts 84 restaurants up for sale
articles.content_orig:
California Pizza Kitchen co-founder Rick Rosenfield told Fox News Digital how two former prosecutors built a pizza empire and how he believes the iconic chain is moving towards a 'new glory.'
A major KFC franchise operator has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection as declining sales, mounting debt and a dispute over unpaid franchise fees threaten its restaurant operations.
Tasty Chick’n, LLC, a Plano, Texas-based franchisee operating 84 KFC and KFC/Taco Bell locations across 10 states, filed for bankruptcy protection on Nov. 16 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas.
The company, which employs approximately 1,646 workers, is seeking to sell its restaurants through a court-supervised process, according to a declaration filed by President and CEO Thomas Scott.
Tasty Chick’n has struggled with falling sales and shrinking profit margins. Restaurant sales declined approximately 15.6% over three years, while profit margins fell from 11.8% in fiscal 2023 to 4% so far in fiscal 2026.
MCDONALD'S BRINGS BACK MACAULAY CULKIN FOR ‘HOME ALONE’ MEAL WITH A PIZZA TWIST
A Yum! Brands Inc. Kentucky Fried Chicken (KFC) restaurant stands in Norwell, Massachusetts, on Thursday, July 25, 2019. (Scott Eisen/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The financial strain led the operator to defer franchise royalty payments in mid-2025 before largely stopping payments that November.
KFC and Taco Bell subsequently issued a notice of default in December 2025, followed by a September 2026 notice of intent to terminate the company's franchise agreements.
Miami, Florida, Miami International Airport, airport terminal, KFC, Kentucky Fried Chicken fast food restaurant. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The franchisors claimed Tasty Chick’n owed approximately $15.7 million in unpaid royalties, advertising contributions and other fees, according to the bankruptcy filing.
Losing those agreements would prevent the operator from running its restaurants under the KFC and Taco Bell brands, potentially eliminating the business's value as an operating enterprise, Scott said.
KFC’s next-generation restaurant concepts are designed to create more modern, dynamic and hospitality-driven experiences for guests around the world. (KFC / Fox News)
The franchisee also reported approximately $67.2 million in debt owed to lenders led by MidCap Financial Trust, along with more than $2 million in claims tied to unpaid rent and other lease charges.
The company operates 75 standalone KFC restaurants and nine co-branded KFC/Taco Bell locations, with Florida and Tennessee accounting for 45 of its restaurants.
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
Tasty Chick’n began marketing its restaurants to potential buyers before filing for bankruptcy and is pursuing a sale of the entire business or individual markets, subject to court approval and required franchise consents.
FOX Business reached out to KFC parent company Yum! Brands for comment.

articles.title_orig: Feature: 20 Wii Exclusives You Should Track Down While You Still Can
articles.title_zh: Feature: 20 Wii Exclusives You Should Track Down While You Still Can
articles.content_orig:
Somehow, someway, it's been two whole decades since the Revolution began and an elderly relative who had never played a video game in their life somehow, someway, thrashed you at Wii Sports bowling.
The little system that could went on to sell over 100 million units across its lifetime, which means that 20 years on it's still possible to pick up a good clean one for a reasonable price - something which can't be said for a certain autostereoscopic handheld with a divergent family tree.
It also means that secondhand software is still plentiful for the most part, with much of the system's catalogue still available for not-silly money (plus some for silly money). So today we're rounding up 20 gems to consider picking up for your trusty Wii.
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
If you're just looking for the Best Wii Games™, we've got you covered elsewhere . Here, we're specifically looking for games slightly off the beaten track, games that were either full-on exclusives or, in a couple of cases where I've stretched the definition, are difficult to find anywhere else.
Ready? Let's dive right into things...
Kicking things off with the Batman, Wayforward's take on the Cartoon Network series captured perfectly the audio-visual elements of the show with a ton of amusing dialogue and a fun, animated take on a character that — outside of his Lego iteration — had gotten pretty dark and self-serious in the movies and other games of the era.
Batman: The Brave and the Bold - The Videogame (or Das Videospiel as my German copy has it) offers simple side-scrolling brawling, but the BAM-BOOM-POW energy is infectious, and this is a great one to play with the kids. There was a DS version, although that's single-player only, so stick with Wii.
Steven Spielberg's making a game, everybody! Legendary Hollywood director Steven Spielberg! The moment we heard that, we imagined Indiana Jones -style derring-do, or something with aliens or dinosaurs. We didn't imagine that the title prominently flagged as "A Steven Spielberg / EA Game" would be a physics-based block puzzler/party game in the Jenga mould.
However, 2008's Boom Blox turned out to be an absolute blast, especially with friends, and a game that made great use of the system's unique controller. it absolutely deserves to be revisited.
A sequel, Boom Blox Bash Party , followed in 2009, and that's a good time, too.
Dead Space: Extraction was a prequel to the 360-era sci-fi/survival horror game PS3/360 game, and perhaps benefited from low expectations, but it's a cracking, moody little rail shooter.
This one came to PS3 two years later with Move controller support, but this rail shooter was built for the Wii and made use of one of the system's best features: the IR camera-powered pointer in the Wiimotes. For accuracy and responsiveness, this fairly low-tech solution to pointer controls still trumps the gyro alternative (which constantly needs resetting/recentring) in our book, and this game is worth setting up the sensor bar.

articles.title_orig: World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets
articles.title_zh: World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets
articles.content_orig:
Jack Sim, the founder of World Toilet Day, travels the world promoting access to safe and clean toilets. When NPR photographed him a few years ago — on a toilet, of course — he was glad to oblige even though it was a chilly and windy November day. John Poole/Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption
Twenty-five years ago, Jack Sim was flush with excitement. (Please pardon the pun.)
The Singapore entrepreneur was looking for a meaningful project and came upon this thought from the prime minister: "He said we should measure our graciousness according to the cleanliness of our public toilets," Sim recalls.
Thus was born World Toilet Day. The goal was more than cleanliness. It was access, too — billions of people do not have a safe and sanitary toilet to use.
Enshrined as an official U.N. day in 2013, World Toilet Day aims to get people talking and thinking about a topic that maybe is a taboo in polite conversation.
A rally in India calls for decent sanitation on a past World Toilet Day demonstration. NOAH SEELAM/AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption
World Toilet Day is all about peeing, pooping and addressing menstrual hygiene in a clean and safe manner — followed by the "conveyance" of excreta to a sanitary disposal system, notes Kate Olive Medlicott , the sanitation and waste team leader within the WASH team at the World Health Organization. Human diseases are shed in sewage, so a top-notch sanitation system is critical, says Medlicott. Cholera is linked to sewage. Polio is, too.
This year's World Toilet Day theme is "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." Even though everyone suffers when they can't find a toilet, the menstrual cycle creates additional complications. If schools or offices lack a safe and sanitary place to attend to period needs and to dispose of period products, girls and women may opt to stay home.
There is another gender issue. Sofia Calltorp , the U.N. Women global head of humanitarian action, says: "When women and girls do not have access to safe toilets," they leave their home and look for a public toilet or a secluded space to do their business, often venturing into unsafe areas. "There is a huge impact in terms of being exposed to harassment or violence," Calltorp says. She points to refugee camps as a place where this issue often arises, with unlit toilets that aren't differentiated by gender.
Poo Guru is a character created by the Defeat Diarrheal Disease Initiative in its ongoing campaign to educate the world about sanitation and the need for safe toilets for all. DefeatDD hide caption
In Western Colombo, Sri Lanka, an informational sign urges users not to squat on the seat as though they were using a squat toilet, which often consists of ... a pit. Haag/ullstein bild/via Getty Images hide caption
A sign from Valencia, Spain, is a reminder of how important it is to have access to a safe toilet. Kristina Ketelsen hide caption
Now you might well ask: Has World Toilet Day made a difference?
The toilet titans we interviewed say yes, it has, just by talking about toilets in the public arena. The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.
What are the next steps? Kellogg Schwab , who specializes in water and wastewater contaminants of public health concern at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, stresses that governments should be a force for change but that it shouldn't be top down. It should also be … oh, forgive me again … bottom up. Schwab suggests giving money to communities to figure out what solutions they can come up with to improve the toilet and sanitation situation. There will be flops. But there will be successes that can be scaled up.
Sand artist Sudarsan Pattnaik created this sculpture in honor of World Toilet Day on a beach in the coastal city of Puri in India. Like the contents of a toilet connected to a sanitation system, it was ... washed away. NurPhoto/via Getty Images hide caption
So maybe one day — Medlicott of WHO thinks in 50 years or so —- Earthlings will look back and say, How curious that in a world of wealth there were not enough safe and secure toilets.
Let's end by reflecting on the present day.
"World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year," says Medlicott. "People find it fun and funny but it's really important to celebrate and act on something we take for granted."
If you're among the population where toilets are plentiful, she suggests pausing to think of a moment — it's happened to all of us — when you needed a bathroom and couldn't find one. Maybe that incident has turned into a funny story you share with friends. Now imagine if it were to happen every day.
I am deeply thankful that all I need to do is walk down the office hallway to find a clean and private loo.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu Associates Acknowledge Role in Setting Off Election Day Arrests
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu Associates Acknowledge Role in Setting Off Election Day Arrests
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing calls from lawmakers for an investigation following a report that alleged that a member of his staff provided information to police against Arab citizens in an attempt to influence last month’s elections. The claims, which Netanyahu’s office denies, were made on an Israeli TV news show this weekend.
The controversy centers on the widely publicized arrest of three activists from the Arab party Raam in southern Israel early on the morning of the October 27 election over an alleged cash-for-votes scheme. Throughout the day, Netanyahu and his Likud party repeatedly amplified the arrests to mobilize their own voters, alleging Raam was trying to “steal the elections.”
Courts later rejected police requests to keep the suspects in custody, saying that the arrests were carried out without a valid search or arrest warrant. All suspects have since then been released.
According to an investigation by Channel 12’s “Uvda,” the allegation originated in Netanyahu’s office. The day before the elections, the report alleges, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, bypassed standard reporting channels and personally contacted the police commissioner to alert him about the activists, passing on information.
Norden allegedly referred police to a separate source who was said to hold information about the activists. But the source was a former employee of the Prime Minister’s Office, the report said.
Based on Norden’s complaint and the information provided by the former employee, police carried out the arrests on election day, the report alleged.
The head of Israel’s Central Elections Committee said in a statement Tuesday that “there is no evidence of election bribery paid to voters on a scale that could affect the election results.” The committee said the investigation into the “many suspicions” raised by the allegations was ongoing, but the effort had shifted to “security related aspects … which are not at the core of the election process and its results.”
On Monday evening, Israel’s Attorney General said she would hold a discussion on the transfer of information from the Prime Minister’s Office to the police. “As part of the discussion, all aspects relating to the matter will be examined,” the Attorney General’s spokesperson said in a statement.
Netanyahu’s office strongly denied the Channel 12 report, saying it was “false and grounds for libel,” but confirmed that Nordan had passed information to the police.
“Criminal information reached Chief of Staff Ido Norden, he fulfilled his duty as expected of any law-abiding citizen and connected that person to the police,” his office said in a statement Sunday evening. Norden learned on the morning of the elections that a person “was indeed caught with tens of thousands of shekels in cash and Raam slips,” the statement continued, referring to a suspect who had already been released.
In a statement, Israel Police said it would examine “the decision-making processes, the chain of reporting, the working interfaces between the relevant police units, and the division of responsibility” related to the allegations in the Channel 12 report. “All police actions, including the operation carried out on election morning, were taken out of commitment and transparency toward the public, and with the aim of protecting the integrity of the elections,” police said.
On Monday evening, the Attorney General requested a pause in this examination until there is a decision “on the appropriate format for the inquiry.”
The main opposition party is calling for an immediate investigation. Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of Yashar and a candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said the conduct of Netanyahu and his circle is “a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” warning that “as long as Netanyahu is in office, there will be no more fair and proper elections in Israel.”
Israel faces political chaos as Netanyahu’s grip on power weakens. What will it take to end the disarray?
Two Arab parties that saw record voter turnout in the elections also demanded an immediate criminal investigation.
“The arrest of our activists in the Negev on the morning of the elections and the attempt to silence Arab Knesset members, if proven, is a direct attack on the integrity of the elections and the will of the voters,” Raam said in a statement, referring to Israel’s parliament. The Joint List called to establish an independent commission of inquiry – the state’s highest investigative body – and suspend all involved police and Shin Bet officials.
“Netanyahu tried to steal our vote, but our vote is what will bring him down. His place is not in the Prime Minister’s Office, but in the interrogation room and before the court,” the party said in a statement.
Since losing his parliamentary majority in the October 27 vote, Netanyahu and his allies have raised various allegations against the Arab parties, accusing them of bribery, foreign funding, and fraud. David Zini, the director of the Shin Bet domestic security service and a Netanyahu loyalist, has pressed to investigate Arab politicians over allegations of foreign interference, but so far hasn’t presented any public evidence to support the allegations against them. According to the Channel 12 report, Zini demanded to wiretap five Arab lawmakers before election day.
The request was refused at the last minute by the attorney general because he did not present any evidence to back his request, Channel 12 reported.
In a statement, the Shin Bet said it carried out “various activities in accordance with its powers under the law.”
Avigdor Liberman, the leader of the Yisrael Beitenu party and the interim chair of the crucial Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, said on Monday that he would summon the Shin Bet and police chiefs to discuss alleged foreign interference attempts in the election.

articles.title_orig: NC utilities commissioner resigns days after Duke Energy rate hike decisions
articles.title_zh: NC utilities commissioner resigns days after Duke Energy rate hike decisions
articles.content_orig:
A North Carolina utilities commissioner who pushed for lower shareholder returns for Duke Energy and stronger protections against data center costs is stepping down.
State Treasurer Brad Briner announced Wednesday that he accepted the resignation of Donald van der Vaart, effective Jan. 1, 2027, the same day Duke's rate increases and utility merger take effect after being approved Monday.
Van der Vaart is leaving four and a half years before his term was scheduled to expire. The announcement did not provide a reason for his departure.
“I appreciate Don’s willingness to serve on the Utilities Commission and wish him the best,” Briner said in a statement.
Van der Vaart did not participate in Monday's Duke Energy Carolinas rate decision and issued a partial dissent in the Duke Energy Progress case.
He was also unable to participate in the commission's decision on Duke's long-term energy plan after missing evidentiary hearings while on vacation.
In his partial dissent, van der Vaart advocated for a lower return on shareholder equity than the approved 9.8% and raised concerns about residential customers being left to pay for power plants that could outlast data center contracts by decades.
The commission approved residential rate increases of roughly 9% over two years, along with new financial requirements for large energy users intended to protect other customers from shouldering their costs.
Van der Vaart joined the commission in April 2025 after being nominated by Briner, a Republican.
Republican lawmakers previously changed the commission's appointment structure, reducing its membership from seven to five and shifting appointment power away from the governor.
His departure opens a seat on the commission just weeks before Democrats are set to take control of the state House.
Briner said he would announce an appointment to fill the vacancy in the coming days or weeks.
Van der Vaart, an engineer and attorney, previously served as secretary of the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality and on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Scientific Advisory Board.

articles.title_orig: China's Xi says US should do 'right thing' on Taiwan to avoid setbacks in relations
articles.title_zh: China's Xi says US should do 'right thing' on Taiwan to avoid setbacks in relations
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan yesterday said it is in “close contact” with the US ahead of today’s talks between the leaders of the US, China and Russia at the APEC Leaders’ Summit and views positively any effort that helps manage the risks of authoritarian expansion.
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to hold an unprecedented three-way meeting on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen, China.
China has been ramping up its military pressure, while Russia this week sent two military aircraft down Taiwan’s east coast.
Photo: Chu Pei-hsiung, Taipei Times
Taiwan is in “close contact with the US and has a full grasp of developments,” Presidential Office spokeswoman Karen Kuo (郭雅慧) said.
Taiwan “views positively any effort that helps manage the risks of authoritarian expansion and contributes to regional security and stability,” she added in a statement.
While the US is Taiwan’s most important international backer, Trump in May said after meeting Xi in Beijing that he was holding back on a new arms sale for Taipei, describing it as a good “bargaining chip.”
Kuo said Taiwan’s position has always been consistent: to strengthen its self-defense, do its utmost to keep the “status quo” from being undermined and continue working with international democratic partners to jointly safeguard regional security.
Relations between Taipei and Beijing are extremely tense. China refuses to talk to President William Lai (賴清德), saying he is a “separatist,” while its military operates around Taiwan on a daily basis.
APEC is one of the few international bodies Taiwan belongs to, although it does not send its president to meetings to avoid political problems.
Taiwan’s envoy to the summit, Acer Group (宏碁) founder and honorary chairman Stan Shih (施振榮), said at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport before flying to Shenzhen that Taiwan is an indispensable partner in global tech, and that he would “engage actively” with the countries attending.
“Taiwan will go with a smile,” Shih added.
“Taiwan is an indispensable partner in the global technology and AI industries and their supply chains, and a trusted partner in the Asia-Pacific region,” he said.
The rapid development of AI and digital technology is reshaping industries and creating opportunities and challenges across the region, Shih said.
Taiwan’s government and businesses could collaborate and invest overseas to expand the AI industry and enable more partners to benefit from its growth, he added.
The meeting marks Shih’s return as Taiwan’s representative nearly two decades after he attended the 2007 summit in Sydney.
At that summit, he proposed the APEC Digital Opportunity Center 2.0 initiative, aimed at narrowing the digital divide among member economies through public-private cooperation
Ahead of this year’s summit, Taiwan repeatedly complained of Chinese efforts to “belittle” its attendance and demanded written guarantees from Beijing that this will not happen.
“We handle the participation of the Taiwan region in APEC-related activities in accordance with the one China principle, the relevant APEC memorandums of understanding, and established practice,” China’s Taiwan Affairs Office spokesman, Chen Binhua (陳斌華), told reporters in Beijing yesterday.
Lai last week said that Taiwan is taking part in the summit on an “equal basis.”
Chen declined to comment on whether the trilateral meeting would touch upon Taiwan.
Taiwanese envoys have interacted with Xi at other APEC summits, although mostly that does not go beyond a polite handshake or a wave.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin Meet for Their First Summit: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin Meet for Their First Summit: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump, right, Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP hide caption
SHENZHEN, China and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday – capping two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even as the men who led them had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.
"History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," said Xi in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."
Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."
"In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.
Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders offering divergent agendas going in:
Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.
There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to steal high end Nvidia chips.
In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.
Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi, and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.
Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.
Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.
"Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.
"We've known each other for a long time," added Trump after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."
Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."
Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.
The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.
For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.
Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.
Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.
Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.
Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.
Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.
The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.
Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches— both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.
From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi, and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.
In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.
Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.
Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.
The catch: his Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.
Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.
Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.
Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.
Following Trump's meeting with Putin, a Kremlin aide would only say that Ukraine had been the focus of the discussions — adding the Kremlin leader had left "in an excellent mood."
Just hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a missile strike on the lone bridge linking mainland Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula for the third time this week — effectively disabling the structure for months to come.
The bridge is widely considered the Russian leader's pet project — a symbol of Russia's claim to territory illegally seized from Ukraine in 2014 rendered in steel.

articles.title_orig: China and Russia say they and US agree on UN reforms, boosting fuel supplies, dialogue on nuclear
articles.title_zh: China and Russia say they and US agree on UN reforms, boosting fuel supplies, dialogue on nuclear
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has repeatedly placed nonproliferation near the top of the agenda for his trilateral meeting Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin , although his counterparts have expressed little interest in committing to new limitations on their nuclear arsenals.
Trump has been pushing for China to join the U.S. and Russia in a new nuclear arms control agreement since his first term in office. Still, he has sought to limit expectations for any major progress in Shenzhen, China, where the world’s top three nuclear powers are meeting on the sidelines of a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders .
Russia suspended its participation in New START, its last remaining nuclear arms pact with the U.S., when it invaded Ukraine in 2022, denying inspections of its nuclear sites. Ahead of the treaty’s expiration this past February , Russia said it would keep to the deal’s limitations on its arsenal for another year, but Trump insisted a new agreement must include China and possibly other nuclear powers.
China has said an arms control agreement should remain between the U.S. and Russia, which together hold nearly 90% of the world’s nuclear arsenal with more than 5,000 warheads each. China has about 600, according to Pentagon estimates, though by 2030 it could have up to 1,000 if its arsenal continues to expand at the current rate.
“China is building up its nuclear arsenal to a very significant degree, and it will continue to do so, and wants to continue to do so,” David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told reporters Wednesday.
The Chinese foreign ministry has declined to say whether nuclear arms control will be discussed at the trilateral meeting on Thursday, with spokesperson Mao Ning saying earlier this week that the three leaders “will have an in-depth exchange of views on important issues bearing on global peace.”
In a call last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearization,” according to a U.S. readout of the call. The Chinese readout made no reference to such a discussion.
Trump has admitted that it will be difficult to get Russia and China to consider reducing their nuclear arsenals.
“So we’re going to talk about denuclearization. Tough subject because it’s very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes, right? But especially since you do have other countries,” he said Monday. “But we’re going to be talking about denuclearization.”
Even in the hours leading up to this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, the world’s top two nuclear powers were making shows of force. On Tuesday, the U.S. launched an unarmed intercontinental ballistic missile in a previously unannounced test at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Hours later, Russia landed two strategic bombers in Vietnam to coincide with Putin’s arrival in China.
While one meeting is not likely to produce dramatic breakthroughs, it could kickstart a process that leads to sustained, formal bilateral or multilateral negotiations on nuclear risk reduction, arms control and disarmament, said Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Washington-based Arms Control Association.
“A top priority for all three leaders should be to head off a costly, escalatory nuclear arms race involving the further buildup of nuclear forces and the resumption of nuclear testing by any state,” he said.
Da Wei, director of the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, said nuclear arms control was not a “proper topic” for the trilateral meeting given the complexity of the issue and how little time Trump, Putin and Xi will have together.
But if the three leaders “can say something about nuclear stability, like a nuclear war is not winnable and should not be fought, I think that will be helpful,” he said in an interview Wednesday.
Rubio has acknowledged that a new agreement could take some time.
“Past agreements, including New START, took years to negotiate and were built upon decades of precedent. They were also between two powers, not three or more,” he wrote on Substack in February. “However, just because something is hard does not mean we should not pursue it or settle for less.”
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

articles.title_orig: Trump: ‘We spy on China, they spy on us’
articles.title_zh: Trump: ‘We spy on China, they spy on us’
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SHENZHEN, China — President Trump has begun an extraordinary visit to Shenzhen, where he is set to join the leaders of Russia and China — two of Washington’s principal geopolitical rivals — for an unprecedented trilateral summit Thursday.
Chinese President Xi Jinping personally welcomed Trump on the tarmac upon his arrival, reciprocating a rare honor Trump extended to him during his September visit to Washington.
All three leaders attended a dinner alongside other regional heads of government on Wednesday night, participating in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.
The trilateral meeting will be the first of its kind by leaders of the United States, Russia and China, three nations with the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
But while Trump has embraced a strategy of diplomatic engagement with historic foes, the three leaders enter the meeting with starkly different agendas.
Russian President Vladimir Putin hopes to secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine. Trump says he would like to discuss a nuclear arms control agreement and his war in Iran. And Xi aims to present China as a superpower on the international stage, capable of forging world peace.
Meeting with Putin before Trump arrived, Xi said that China’s relationship with Russia had remained as steadfast “as a rock through wind and rain.”
The two sides, he said, would pursue a “multipolar world” — a vision for a global balance of power that would see American influence weakened across Europe and Asia.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit.
Trump, for his part, has hedged on his expectations of the summit, signaling resolve against China ahead of his arrival here.
On Monday, the Trump administration tightened export controls on semiconductor chips essential to artificial intelligence development, closing loopholes aimed at curbing Chinese efforts to circumvent restrictions — a move that Trump acknowledged might be an “insult” to Xi before the meeting.
Chinese officials said Wednesday afternoon that Beijing reserved the right to retaliate.
“In essence, the United States is simultaneously trying to find limited avenues of cooperation with China while trying to clamp down on their access to critical parts of the AI supply chain, which doesn’t set up the conditions for productive dialogue,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump also met in Manila on Tuesday with fellow members of the Quad — India, Japan and Australia — in a show of resolve toward Beijing.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in the Philippines.
“We continue to protect peace through strength,” he added.
